content.text:
**Choice: candidate 6**, which orders about 1.1× the forecast every day. I worked this out by hand, on rough averages; I didn't simulate it step by step.

**What the plans are.** Candidates 2, 6, 0/3 and 1 order the forecast demand for the day their order arrives (lead time 3 days for good 0, 2 for good 1), scaled by about 1.0×, 1.1×, 1.2× and 1.3×. Candidate 0 is the 1.2× plan with smaller orders over the last few days. Candidates 4, 5 and 7 order in large batches every 2–3 days.

**Where the plans lose:**
- **Days 0–2 (all plans).** Starting stock is short: good 0 has 44 units against 107 of demand before day 3, and good 1 has 56 against 83 before day 2. Every plan pays the same penalty here.
- **Below 1.046×.** The demand multiplier averages 1.046, so candidate 2 (1.0×) runs down its stock on average. It pays steady penalties: 14 per unit of good 0 (lost margin 8 plus penalty 6) and 11 per unit of good 1 (9 plus 2).
- **Above 1.046×.** Stock builds up instead. At 1.2× it grows by roughly 4.6 units a day for good 0 and 7 for good 1. That means:
  - Holding costs in the order of 1,500 over the month, against about 800 at 1.1×.
  - By day 29 the plan is close to the 264-unit storage limit, and units above it are lost.
  - Up to 100–200 units left at the end are worth nothing, at roughly 10–12 each. Candidate 0's smaller final orders only take back part of this.
  - Candidate 1 (1.3×) has the same problems, only worse.
- **1.1× (candidate 6).** Stock grows slowly, by about 1.7 and 2.4 units a day. That builds a buffer against random demand of roughly ±30% a day, with modest holding costs and leftovers.
- **Batch plans (4, 5, 7).** Ordering less often saves only 30 per skipped day. In return they hold much more stock, use most of the storage, and run out between batches when demand jumps. Overall that costs more than it saves.

**Effect of randomness.** Daily demand varies by about ±9 units for good 0 and ±13 for good 1. A shortage costs about as much as a leftover unit (14 vs 12 for good 0, 11 vs 10 for good 1). So the best level is a small buffer, enough to avoid most shortages without carrying a large unsold stock to the end. Candidate 6 strikes that balance best and should have the highest expected profit.

**Выбор: кандидат 5** — по ожидаемой прибыли он, по-моему, лучший. Уверенность средняя: отрыв от кандидата 6 небольшой. Считал прикидками в уме, полной пошаговой симуляции нет.

**Что это за планы.** Каждый план — прогноз спроса, сдвинутый на срок поставки и умноженный на коэффициент.
- Каждый день заказывают: кандидат 2 (×1,0), 6 (×1,1), 0 (×1,2, с урезанным концом), 3 (×1,2) и 1 (×1,3).
- Раз в два дня заказывают: кандидат 5 (×1,1) и 7 (×1,2).
- Раз в три дня заказывает кандидат 4.
- Нехватка в дни 0–2 одинакова у всех: первые заказы приходят не раньше дня 2–3.

**Какой коэффициент лучше.**
- Средний множитель спроса около 1,046. При ×1,0 запас в среднем отстаёт от спроса. Неустойки выходят дорогими: каждая недостающая единица стоит 14 для товара 0 и 11 для товара 1.
- Излишек переходит на следующие дни. Партии продаются от старых к новым, а годность 9 и 7 дней, поэтому небольшой излишек почти не списывается и работает как страховой запас.
- При ×1,1 излишек около 5 % в день. Это даёт защиту примерно в 2 стандартных отклонения дневного спроса, а к концу остаётся немного непроданного (примерно 40 ед. товара 0 и 66 ед. товара 1).
- При ×1,2–1,3 излишек 15–25 %. Растут хранение, списания и остаток в конце, который ничего не стоит.
- Вывод: разумнее всего ×1,1.

**Каждый день или раз в два дня.**
- Ежедневный заказ — это 28 дней по 30 = 840 на фиксированных платах.
- Заказ раз в два дня — 14 × 30 = 420, экономия 420.
- Взамен растёт хранение: в среднем лежит лишних полдня спроса. Это примерно 4,2 в день по товару 0 и 9,2 по товару 1, всего около 13,4 в день, или около 360 за период.
- Итог: около +60 в пользу кандидата 5. Кроме того, спрос за два дня колеблется относительно меньше (около 21 % против 30 %), поэтому тот же запас ×1,1 защищает лучше.

**Почему не кандидат 4.** Раз в три дня хранение растёт примерно до 740 при экономии около 540 на фиксированных платах. Ещё есть риск переполнения склада: в день 26 приходят 202 единицы товара 1 сверх уже лежащего запаса, а склад вмещает 264.

I pick **Candidate 5**. It and Candidate 6 come out nearly even, and Candidate 5 is ahead by an estimated ~70. I worked this out in my head on rough averages, not with an exact simulation.

**What each plan is.** Candidate 2 orders exactly the forecast, timed for the lead time (for example, 28 = forecast for day 3, product 0). The other plans scale that forecast:
- Candidate 6 orders ~1.1× the forecast, Candidate 3 ~1.2× and Candidate 1 ~1.3×, all every day.
- Candidate 0 is the 1.2× plan, but its last few orders are cut by about 0.9×.
- Candidates 5 and 7 order every 2 days at 1.1× and 1.2×.
- Candidate 4 orders every 3 days at 1.1×.

**Losses common to all.** The first days are short for every plan, since starting stock (44 and 56) runs out before the first orders arrive. A plan can't avoid this.

**How much to over-order.** Average demand is 1.046× the forecast, not 1×.
- **1.0× (Candidate 2):** it falls behind demand every day, so shortages pile up. Each missed unit costs about 14 for product 0 and 11 for product 1 (lost margin plus penalty). This plan is clearly the weakest.
- **1.1×:** stock builds up slowly, about 4 units a day. That cushion absorbs most of the swings (roughly ±30% a day). Expected total shortage is about 64 units.
- **1.2× and above (Candidates 0, 3, 7, 1):** shortage drops to about 23 units. In exchange, about 80 extra units are bought and wasted (~880), and holding the bigger stock costs about 700 more. The shortage saving is only about 1,000, so these plans come out roughly 500–600 behind 1.1×. Candidate 0's end-of-plan cuts help, but not enough to close that gap. At 1.3×, combined stock also gets close to the 264-unit limit.

**How often to order (comparing the 1.1× plans).**
- **Every 2 days (Candidate 5):** 14 order days instead of 28 saves about 420 in daily order fees. Holding the extra stock between orders costs about 0.5 × (28·0.3 + 42·0.4) ≈ 12.6 a day, about 350 in total. Net, it is about +70 ahead of Candidate 6. Deliveries of the two products land on alternating days, so the warehouse limit is not a problem.
- **Every 3 days (Candidate 4):** the extra holding cost (~27 a day) is bigger than the fee saving (~20 a day). Morning stock also comes close to 264, so some deliveries could be lost.

**Ranking:** 5 ≳ 6 > 0 ≈ 3 ≈ 7 > 1, 4 > 2.

Candidate 5's lead over Candidate 6 is small compared with the random variation in demand.

**Choice: Candidate 2** (moderate confidence). I estimated this in my head with a rough random-walk model, not a full day-by-day simulation, so the numbers below are approximate.

**What the candidates are.** Candidate 2 orders exactly the forecast each day, timed so it arrives when needed: q0 = mu[t+3][0] and q1 = mu[t+2][1]. The other daily plans are the same pattern scaled up: Candidate 6 by about ×1.1, Candidates 0 and 3 by about ×1.2 (Candidate 0 cuts its last few orders), and Candidate 1 by about ×1.3. Candidates 5 and 7 bundle two days' demand into one order (about ×1.1 and ×1.2). Candidate 4 bundles three days' demand at about ×1.1.

**Why I ruled out the larger plans:**
1. **Unsold demand is lost, not carried forward.** When stock runs out, the missed sales simply disappear. So even ordering at the forecast, stock tends to build up a cushion on its own over the month.
2. **Every unit beyond the true average demand (about 1.046 × forecast) mostly ends up as leftover stock.** Leftovers are worth nothing at the end, so each one wastes its purchase price (12 for item 0, 10 for item 1).
3. **×1.2–1.3 plans pile up stock fast.** That is roughly +4 units a day of item 0 and +7 a day of item 1 at ×1.2, more at ×1.3. That means about 100–200+ units left over, possible loss of deliveries when the 264-unit limit is hit, and higher storage costs. They lose thousands. Candidate 0's smaller final orders take only about 10 units off the leftover.
4. **×1.1 vs ×1.0 (Candidate 6 vs 2).** I treated stock as a random walk over about 27 days with daily swings of about 8 units (item 0) and 14 units (item 1).
   - Ordering ×1.1 saves about 28 units of item 0 and 42 of item 1 from going short. That is worth about 730 + 880 in sales and avoided penalties.
   - But the extra purchases cost about 876 + 1260.
   - Higher average stock adds about 600 in storage.
   - Net: Candidate 2 comes out ahead by roughly 1,000.
5. **Batch ordering.** Candidate 5 saves about 420 in daily order fees (30 per ordering day), but its bigger deliveries add about 390 in storage. On top of that it carries the same ×1.1 overstock, so it still trails Candidate 2. Candidate 4 (three-day batches) adds even more storage, and when large item-1 and item-0 deliveries land on consecutive days, the 264-unit limit could cut a delivery.

**Robustness.** Candidate 2 holds the least stock, so nothing expires and the space limit is never at risk. Shortages from random demand swings are partly cushioned by the stock that builds up on its own. The cost of overstocking falls hardest on the larger plans.

I pick **candidate 5**, but only by a narrow margin. My estimates put candidates 5, 6 and 2 close together. I checked them by hand on average demand, so the gap is within my error.

**Candidates 0–3 and 6 order every day.** Each orders a fixed multiple of the demand forecast, shifted by the lead time:
- **Multiples:** candidate 2 orders 1.0× the forecast, 6 orders 1.1×, 3 orders 1.2× and 1 orders 1.3×. Candidate 0 orders 1.2× but cuts to about 0.9× for its last few orders, from day 23 on.
- **Fixed cost:** 28 order days × 30 = 840 each.
- **Average demand:** it runs about 4.6% above forecast. Unsold demand isn't carried over, so the stock surplus only grows over time.
- **1.2× and 1.3× (candidates 1, 3, 0):** these build a surplus of roughly 4–7 units a day per product. By the end that is about 300 units, which costs holding fees, is thrown away unused, and pushes against the 264-unit warehouse limit. Candidate 0's cut at the end only uses up about 40 of that surplus. These three are clearly worse.
- **1.0× (candidate 2) vs 1.1× (candidate 6):** at 1.0× the stock drifts down and shortages pile up, roughly 50–100 units per product. At 1.1× shortages drop to about 10–40 units, at the price of about 70 and 120 extra units bought and a larger leftover. Weighing the units bought, lost sales with their penalties, and holding, 1.1× comes out ahead by about 0 to 120. That is essentially a tie.

**Candidates 4, 5 and 7 order in batches:**
- **Candidate 4 (every 3 days, 1.1×):** it pays 300 in fixed costs, saving 540 against daily ordering. But it holds stock for one or two extra nights each cycle, which costs about 780. Its large orders of the second product (166 and 202 units) also overflow the warehouse. Worse than daily ordering.
- **Candidate 7 (every 2 days, 1.2×):** same surplus problem as the other 1.2× plans.
- **Candidate 5 (every 2 days, 1.1×):** it pays 420 in fixed costs, saving 420 against candidate 6. The extra night of holding costs about 380. Each delivery covers two days, so the second day's goods are on the shelf a day early, and there are slightly fewer shortages.
- **Candidate 5's risk:** the warehouse may overflow on days 26 and 28, by about 25–35 units of the second product. Those units are mostly surplus that would be thrown away at the end anyway, so the loss is small.

So candidate 5 comes out roughly 40 or more ahead of 6, with 2 close behind. Given how small that gap is, returning "don't know" (−1) would also have been defensible.

I picked **candidate 0**. This is a rough estimate worked out in my head, not a full step-by-step simulation.

1. **Where the plans differ.** Candidates 2, 6, 0, 3 and 1 all order every day. They differ mainly in scale: about 1.0×, 1.1×, 1.2×, 1.2× and 1.3× the forecast, shifted by each product's lead time. Candidates 4, 5 and 7 batch their orders every 2–3 days.
2. **Starting shortage.** The opening stock (44 and 56) can't cover demand until the first deliveries arrive, so every plan pays the same early penalties. It doesn't separate the candidates.
3. **Expected demand runs above forecast.** The demand multiplier averages about 1.046, and a shortage costs a lot: 8 lost margin + 6 penalty for product 0, and 9 + 2 for product 1. So plans at 1.0–1.1× still run short often.
4. **About 1.2× builds a buffer.** It grows by roughly 4–6 units a day per product. Because stock sells oldest-first, that buffer almost never reaches the shelf-life limit within 30 days, so the main cost is storage. At 1.3× (candidate 1), the extra stock adds more storage cost and pushes toward the 264-unit warehouse limit.
5. **The end of the horizon decides between 0 and 3.** Leftover stock on day 29 is worthless. Candidate 0 matches candidate 3 until day 22, then orders below forecast at the end (for example 16, 21, 22, 26 of product 0 instead of 22, 28, 29, 35), so it uses up its buffer. Candidate 3 keeps ordering at 1.2× and ends with unsold stock it has already paid for. That should cost roughly several hundred to over a thousand.
6. **Batch plans (4, 5, 7).** They save on the 30-per-day order fee (about 450–600 in total), but carry more stock between deliveries, which costs about the same in storage. Large single deliveries also risk overflowing the 264-unit warehouse. None of them cut back near the end.

Overall, candidate 0 should have the highest expected profit: it is protected against shortages through the middle of the month and leaves little waste at the end.

I estimate **candidate 5** has the highest expected profit. Its edge over candidate 6 is small: it saves about 60, which is inside my rough estimating error. I worked through the cost structure by hand at forecast values rather than simulating each day.

**How the plans are built.** Candidates 0, 1, 2, 3 and 6 order every day. Each order is the forecast demand on its arrival day times a fixed ratio: 1.0 for candidate 2, about 1.1 for candidate 6, about 1.2 for candidates 0 and 3, and about 1.3 for candidate 1. For example, candidate 0's day-0 order of 34 units of good 0 arrives on day 3, where the forecast is 28 (34/28 ≈ 1.2). Candidates 5 and 7 order every two days, at about 1.1 and 1.2 of the forecast for the days each batch covers. Candidate 4 orders every three days at about 1.1.

**Choosing the ratio.**
- A shortfall costs much more than a surplus. A missed unit costs 8 + 6 = 14 for good 0 and 9 + 2 = 11 for good 1. Leftover stock carries over to the next days (oldest sold first) and only matters when it spoils.
- Average demand is 1.046 × forecast. So candidate 2's ratio of 1.0 runs a steady shortfall of about 4.6%. Day-to-day swings add more shortages on top, and each one is expensive.
- A ratio of 1.2 builds up about 15% surplus that ends up spoiled. For good 0 alone that comes to roughly 12 × 0.15 × 28 × 27 ≈ 1,360. This rules out candidates 0, 1, 3 and 7.
- A ratio of 1.1 gives a small safety margin, and its spoilage is about 5% of purchases. That leaves candidates 6, 5 and 4.
- Nothing can fix the first days. The starting stock (44 of good 0, 56 of good 1) is below the forecast demand before the first deliveries arrive, so every plan starts short.

**Daily versus batched ordering at 1.1.**
- Candidate 6 pays the 30 fee on 28 days, which is 840. Candidate 5 pays it on 14 days, which is 420, so it saves 420.
- In exchange, candidate 5 keeps the second day's stock overnight. That is about 30 × 0.3 + 42 × 0.4 ≈ 26 per two-day period, or about 360 over 14 periods. The net is about +60 in favour of candidate 5.
- Ordering two days at once also evens out some of the demand swings, and capacity (264) is not a constraint here.
- Candidate 4 saves another 120 in fees (10 order days), but carrying stock for three days costs more than that.
- Candidate 5's last orders also fit the end of the horizon: on day 26 it orders 32 of good 0 against a forecast of 29 on day 29, and 140 of good 1 against 127 for days 28–29.

**Выбор: кандидат 5** (уверенность средняя).

**Что это за планы.**
- Кандидаты 2, 6, 0/3, 1 заказывают каждый день прогноз дня прихода, умноженный на коэффициент: 1,0 / 1,1 / 1,2 / 1,3.
- Кандидат 0 отличается от 3 только тем, что в последние дни урезает заказы примерно до 0,9× прогноза.
- Кандидаты 5 и 7 заказывают раз в 2 дня с коэффициентом 1,1 и 1,2. Кандидат 4 заказывает раз в 3 дня с коэффициентом 1,1.

**Потери, которых не избежать.** Товара 0 до первой поставки на 3-й день не хватает: спрос за дни 0–2 около 107, а на складе 44. Товара 1 не хватает в день 1. В этом все планы одинаковы.

**Сколько стоит лишняя единица.** Остатки не портятся, а переходят на следующий день: при FIFO запас меньше 4 дней спроса не доживает до списания. Поэтому заказ сверх спроса накапливается как запас и почти весь пропадает в конце.
- Единица, которая продалась, приносит 20+6−12 = 14 по товару 0 и 19+2−10 = 11 по товару 1 (маржа плюс избежанная неустойка).
- Единица, которая осталась к концу, теряет 12 и 10 соответственно, плюс хранение.
- Отсюда выгоднее всего, чтобы заказ в среднем совпадал со спросом, то есть был около 1,046× прогноза. Хранение тянет оптимум чуть ниже.

**Оценка кандидатов.**
- **Коэффициенты 1,2 и 1,3 (кандидаты 0, 1, 3, 7).** Избыток копится: по товару 0 примерно на 4 ед. в день, по товару 1 — на 6,5. К концу остаются сотни лишних единиц (порядка 100+ по товару 0), плюс хранение. Урезание в конце у кандидата 0 возвращает лишь около 14 единиц товара 0. Все четыре плана хуже остальных.
- **1,0 против 1,1 (кандидаты 2 и 6).** Оба примерно на 5 % отклоняются от среднего спроса, в разные стороны. По ожидаемому итогу они близки.
- **Заказ раз в 2 дня (кандидат 5).** Дней с заказом 14 вместо 28, экономия фиксированной платы 14 × 30 = 420. Дополнительное хранение — около полудня спроса: примерно 12,6 в день, около 350 за период. В плюсе остаётся примерно +70. Кроме того, партия на 2 дня гасит часть колебаний спроса внутри этих двух дней.
- **Заказ раз в 3 дня (кандидат 4).** Экономия 540, но лишнее хранение около 700. Партии по 100–200 единиц ещё и рискуют упереться во вместимость склада 264.

Кандидат 5 впереди 2 и 6 примерно на 70 из-за экономии на фиксированной плате. При такой случайности спроса это небольшой отрыв, поэтому уверенность только средняя.

I pick **candidate 5**. This is a rough mental estimate, not a day-by-day simulation of each plan, and candidates 5 and 6 are close.

1. **What the daily plans are.** Candidate 2 orders exactly the forecast, shifted by the lead time (for example, its day-0 order for good 0 equals the day-3 forecast of 28). The other daily plans are the same pattern scaled up: candidate 6 by about 1.1×, candidate 3 by about 1.2×, and candidate 1 by about 1.3×. Candidate 0 matches candidate 3 but cuts its last orders to about 0.9×.

2. **Where the losses come from.**
   - The average demand multiplier is about 1.046. So ordering exactly the forecast (candidate 2) leaves stock trending down, and with ±30% swings there are steady lost sales. Each unsold unit costs 8 + 6 = 14 for good 0 and 9 + 2 = 11 for good 1.
   - At 1.2× and above (candidates 0, 1, 3), stock grows by roughly 4 units a day of good 0 and 7 of good 1. Once the buffer stops being useful, the excess spoils, costing about 12 and 10 per unit. Candidate 0's smaller final orders only partly recover this.
   - About 1.1× (candidates 5 and 6) gives a moderate safety buffer with little spoilage. That looks like the best balance.

3. **Ordering every day or in batches.**
   - Candidate 5 is also about 1.1×, but it orders every second day. That means about 14 order days instead of 28, saving about 420 in order fees. The cost is roughly half a day's demand held overnight, about 13 a day in storage, or about 350 over the horizon. That leaves candidate 5 roughly 50–70 ahead of candidate 6.
   - Candidate 7 batches the same way but at about 1.2×, so it carries the overstocking problem.
   - Candidate 4 orders every third day. It saves more in fees, but its storage costs and spoilage risk are higher, and it overstocks as well.

4. **Risk.** Ordering about 1.1× keeps a buffer against high-demand days without overflowing the 264-unit warehouse. Candidate 5's two-day batches don't make it much more sensitive to demand swings than candidate 6.

Candidate 5 should come out slightly ahead of candidate 6, and well ahead of the 1.0× plan (2) and the 1.2–1.3× plans (0, 1, 3, 7).

Я выбрал кандидата 5 с умеренной уверенностью: он наименее явно проигрывает по ожидаемой прибыли. Расчёт прикидочный, в уме, поэтому разрыв с кандидатами 6 и 7 небольшой и неточный.

**Что представляют собой планы.** Все кандидаты — один и тот же прогноз спроса, сдвинутый на срок поставки и умноженный на коэффициент. Отличаются они коэффициентом и частотой заказов:

| Кандидат | Коэффициент | Заказы |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1,0 | ежедневно |
| 6 | 1,1 | ежедневно |
| 3 | 1,2 | ежедневно |
| 0 | 1,2, в последние дни ~0,9 | ежедневно |
| 1 | ~1,3 | ежедневно |
| 5 | 1,1 | раз в 2 дня |
| 7 | 1,2 | раз в 2 дня |
| 4 | 1,1 | раз в 3 дня |

**Какой коэффициент лучше.** Средний множитель спроса — 1,046, поэтому план без запаса (кандидат 2) хронически недопоставляет. Остатки переходят на следующий день, поэтому выпавшие продажи накапливаются. Для товара 1 это около 120 единиц, а каждая стоит 21 (маржа 9 плюс неустойка 2).
- Коэффициент 1,1 сокращает потери продаж. Добавочная закупка и хранение съедают выигрыш почти целиком, так что для товара 1 результат чуть лучше 1,0, для товара 0 — примерно вровень.
- Коэффициент 1,2 копит лишний запас: для товара 0 около 4 единиц в день, для товара 1 около 7. Это растущее хранение и пропавшая закупка в конце, а к концу горизонта возможен упор во вместимость склада 264. Это проигрышный вариант, особенно для товара 0. Поэтому кандидаты 1, 3, 0 и 7 хуже.
- Итог: оптимум около 1,1.

**Какая частота заказов лучше.**
- Ежедневный заказ стоит 28 × 30 = 840 за фиксированные платежи.
- Заказ раз в 2 дня стоит около 420. Добавочный запас на складе — примерно полдня спроса, это около 13 в день хранения, всего примерно 365. Чистый выигрыш около +55, плюс небольшой бонус: накопленный запас частично гасит колебания спроса.
- Заказ раз в 3 дня экономит около 540 на заказах, но добавочное хранение около 730. Получается минус, и есть риск переполнения около дня 26, когда приходит 202 единицы товара 1. Поэтому кандидат 4 хуже.

**Кандидат 5:** коэффициент 1,1, заказ раз в 2 дня, вместимость склада не превышается (на пике примерно 236 из 264). По ожидаемому итогу он немного лучше кандидата 6 и кандидата 7.
